expectedText:
TRANSFER-ON-DEATH DEED
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Morgan

OWNER, BENEFICIARY, AND PROPERTY DECLARATION
Pat Morgan, being the owner of the real property located at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, legally described as Lot 12, Block 3, Tract No. 4567, as per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County Records, creates this Revocable Transfer on Death Deed. Pat Morgan transfers all of Pat Morgan's interest in the described property to Jordan Morgan on Pat Morgan's death. Pat Morgan retains the right to revoke this deed at any time before then, and this deed conveys no present interest in the property to Jordan Morgan. This deed transfers only Pat Morgan's own share of the property; it does not transfer the share of any co-owner of the property.

PROPERTY ELIGIBLE FOR A TOD DEED
California's Revocable Transfer on Death Deed statute applies only to real property that is (1) a parcel of land improved with one to four residential dwelling units, or (2) a residential unit (such as a condominium) and its appurtenant common area within a common interest development. A parcel of agricultural land greater than 40 acres does not qualify, regardless of how it is otherwise improved. The property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, described as Lot 12, Block 3, Tract No. 4567, as per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County Records, is represented to fall within one of the qualifying categories.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), “real property” means either of the following: (1) A parcel of land that is improved with one to four residential dwelling units. (2) A residential separate interest and its appurtenant common area in a common interest development, regardless of the number of separate interests in the common interest development. (b) “Real property” does not include a parcel of agricultural land that is greater than 40 acres in size."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5610, California Probate Code, Revocable Transfer on Death Deed — definition of "real property" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5610.)
  Known gap: This is California's own statutory definition, offered as evidence of how one state defines eligible property — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular property or transfer. Transfer-on-death deeds are a relatively recent and unevenly adopted mechanism: not every state authorizes one, and states that do vary in what property qualifies and under what formalities. Separately, California frames the 40-acre limit as an exclusion from an otherwise-qualifying residential parcel, not as an independent "agricultural property with a single-family residence" category — a distinction worth preserving rather than collapsing into shorthand. Finally, this entire statute (Probate Code Part 4, §§ 5600-5698) is presently scheduled to repeal itself on January 1, 2032 unless a later-enacted statute extends or removes that date; it has been amended several times since 2015 but has not been made permanent as of the most recent amendment located (2023, effective 2024). This is a single statutory section (§ 5610); no additional independent source was found for this.

REVOCABILITY AND NO PRESENT TRANSFER DURING OWNER'S LIFETIME
During Pat Morgan's lifetime, executing and recording this deed does not affect Pat Morgan's ownership of the property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814. Pat Morgan may sell, mortgage, lease, or otherwise deal with the property without Jordan Morgan's consent, and the property remains subject to Pat Morgan's creditors as though this deed had not been made. Jordan Morgan holds no legal or equitable interest in the property, and the property is not reachable by Jordan Morgan's creditors, unless and until the deed operates at Pat Morgan's death.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "During the transferor’s life, execution and recordation of a revocable transfer on death deed: (a) Does not affect the ownership rights of the transferor, and the transferor or the transferor’s agent or other fiduciary may convey, assign, contract, encumber, or otherwise deal with the property, and the property is subject to process of the transferor’s creditors, as if no revocable transfer on death deed were executed or recorded. (b) Does not create any legal or equitable right in the beneficiary, and the property is not subject to process of the beneficiary’s creditors. (c) Does not transfer or convey any right, title, or interest in the property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5650, California Probate Code, effect during transferor's life (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5650.)
  Known gap: This describes California's own statutory rule for revocable TOD deeds specifically, not a general statement about how every deed-like instrument works, and not a claim about which state's law applies to a given transfer — TOD-deed statutes are not uniform across the states that have them. This is a single statutory section (§ 5650); no additional independent source was found for this.

STATUTORY FORM AND EXECUTION FORMALITIES
This deed must be substantially in the statutory form, signed and dated by Pat Morgan, signed by two witnesses present together who either watch Pat Morgan sign or hear Pat Morgan acknowledge the signature, and acknowledged before a notary public. It is not effective unless it is also recorded in the county where the property is located on or before 60 days after the date it is notarized.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A revocable transfer on death deed is not effective unless all of the following conditions are satisfied: (a) The deed is signed by the transferor and dated. (b) The deed is signed by two witnesses who were present at the same time and who witnessed either the signing of the deed or the transferor’s acknowledgment that the transferor had signed the deed. (c) The deed is acknowledged before a notary public."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5624, California Probate Code, conditions for effectiveness — signing, witnesses, notarization (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5624.)
  "(a) A revocable transfer on death deed is not effective unless the deed is recorded on or before 60 days after the date it was acknowledged before a notary."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5626, California Probate Code, recording deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5626.)
  Known gap: This describes California's specific formalities (two witnesses plus notarization, and a 60-day recording deadline). These requirements are not uniform even among the small number of states that authorize a transfer-on-death or beneficiary deed — some require only notarization and no witnesses, some impose no recording deadline at all, and this is not a claim about which state's formalities apply to a particular deed.

HOW A TOD DEED IS REVOKED
Pat Morgan may revoke this deed at any time before death, without Jordan Morgan's joinder, consent, or agreement, and without giving Jordan Morgan notice. Under California's statute, a recorded TOD deed can be revoked in any of three ways: recording a new TOD deed for the same property (the later-recorded deed controls and revokes the earlier one), recording a separate instrument of revocation executed and recorded with the same formalities as a TOD deed, or selling, giving away, or otherwise transferring the property to someone else before death and recording that transfer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) If a revocable transfer on death deed is recorded for the same property for which another revocable transfer on death deed is recorded, the later executed deed is the operative instrument and its recordation revokes the earlier executed deed."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5628, California Probate Code, later-recorded deed revokes earlier deed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5628.)
  "A transferor who has the capacity to contract may revoke a revocable transfer on death deed at any time."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5630, California Probate Code, revocation at any time (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5630.)
  "(a) An instrument revoking a revocable transfer on death deed shall be executed and recorded in the same manner as execution and recordation of a revocable transfer on death deed. (b) Joinder, consent, or agreement of, or notice to, the beneficiary is not required for revocation of a revocable transfer on death deed."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5632, California Probate Code, instrument of revocation; no beneficiary consent required (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5632.)
  "There are three ways to revoke a recorded TOD deed: (1) Complete, have witnessed and notarized, and RECORD a revocation form. (2) Create, have witnessed and notarized, and RECORD a new TOD deed. (3) Sell or give away the property, or transfer it to a trust, before your death and RECORD the deed. A TOD deed can only affect property that you own when you die."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5642(b), California Probate Code, statutory form — sale or transfer as revocation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5642.)
  Known gap: This is California's specific set of revocation mechanisms, offered as evidence for one state's statute rather than a general or universal description of how transfer-on-death instruments are revoked elsewhere.

MULTIPLE-BENEFICIARY DESIGNATION
Pat Morgan may name more than one beneficiary. If Casey Morgan is named as an additional beneficiary alongside Jordan Morgan, the named beneficiaries take title to the property as tenants in common in equal shares on Pat Morgan's death. California's transfer-on-death deed statute does not provide a separate "contingent" or fallback beneficiary who stands in only if the primary beneficiary predeceases the owner; instead, if a named beneficiary does not survive Pat Morgan, that beneficiary's share is redistributed among the other named beneficiaries who do survive. If no named beneficiary survives Pat Morgan, this deed has no effect, and the property does not pass under it.

BENEFICIARY PREDECEASING THE OWNER
Jordan Morgan's interest under this deed is contingent on surviving Pat Morgan. If Jordan Morgan does not survive Pat Morgan, that interest lapses. If more than one beneficiary is named, the named beneficiaries take the property as tenants in common in equal shares, and a lapsed beneficiary's share is redistributed among the surviving named beneficiaries in equal shares. If every named beneficiary fails to survive Pat Morgan, the deed has no effect and the property does not pass under it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(2) The interest of a beneficiary is contingent on the beneficiary surviving the transferor. Notwithstanding Section 21110, the interest of a beneficiary that fails to survive the transferor lapses. (3) Except as provided in paragraph (4), if there is more than one beneficiary, they take the property as tenants in common, in equal shares. (4) If there is more than one beneficiary, the share of a beneficiary that lapses or fails for any reason is transferred to the others in equal shares."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5652(a), California Probate Code, survivorship condition; lapse; tenants in common; redistribution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5652.)
  "If all beneficiaries die before you, the TOD deed has no effect. If a beneficiary dies before you, but other beneficiaries survive you, the share of the deceased beneficiary will be divided equally between the surviving beneficiaries."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5642(b) [predecease], California Probate Code, statutory form — effect if all beneficiaries predecease (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5642.)
  Known gap: California's statute expressly disapplies its own general anti-lapse rule (Probate Code § 21110, which for wills and certain other instruments can substitute a deceased beneficiary's issue) to a TOD deed — the lapse here is unconditional, with no automatic substitution of the deceased beneficiary's descendants. This is a real, checkable difference from how a lapsed gift under a will is often handled in California, and it is specific to this deed mechanism. The "if every beneficiary fails to survive, the deed has no effect" consequence is drawn from the statute's own mandated explanatory form text rather than from the numbered operative subsections alone. This is California's rule; other states' TOD-deed statutes are not assumed to handle predeceased beneficiaries the same way.

PRIORITY BETWEEN A TOD DEED AND A WILL OR OTHER INSTRUMENT
If this deed and another instrument (such as a will) both purport to dispose of the same property, and the other instrument makes a revocable disposition of it, whichever of the two was executed later controls. If the other instrument instead makes an irrevocable disposition of the property, that instrument controls regardless of which was executed later. California's statutory TOD deed form itself states that a TOD deed cannot be revoked by a will.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) If a revocable transfer on death deed recorded on or before 60 days after the date it was acknowledged before a notary public and another instrument both purport to dispose of the same property: (1) If the other instrument makes a revocable disposition of the property, the later executed of the revocable transfer on death deed or the other instrument is the operative instrument. (2) If the other instrument makes an irrevocable disposition of the property, the other instrument and not the revocable transfer on death deed is the operative instrument."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5660, California Probate Code, conflicting instruments (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5660.)
  "A TOD deed cannot be revoked by will, or by purporting to leave the subject property to anyone via will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5642(b) [will], California Probate Code, statutory form — TOD deed not revocable by will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5642.)
  Known gap: California's operative priority rule (Probate Code § 5660) refers generically to "another instrument" that makes a "revocable" or "irrevocable" disposition — it does not use the word "will" in its own text. A will is generally a revocable disposition under California law, which is why the general later-executed-controls rule is described here as applying to wills, but that characterization is an inference from the general nature of wills, not a direct quotation of § 5660 itself. Separately, the statute's own mandated form language does state directly, in its own words, that a TOD deed cannot be revoked by a will. This is California's rule; other states' TOD/beneficiary-deed statutes may resolve a deed-versus-will conflict differently, or may not address it at all.

JOINT TENANCY AND COMMUNITY PROPERTY INTERACTION
If, at Pat Morgan's death, title to the property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 is held in joint tenancy or as community property with right of survivorship, this deed is void, and the property instead passes according to the right of survivorship. If Pat Morgan holds the property as community property with a spouse, additional statutory requirements governing spousal consent, revocation of consent, or modification of a community-property TOD deed also apply, and are ineffective unless recorded within the time otherwise required for that consent, revocation, or modification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If, at the time of the transferor’s death, title to the property described in the revocable transfer on death deed is held in joint tenancy or as community property with right of survivorship, the revocable transfer on death deed is void. The transferor’s interest in the property is governed by the right of survivorship and not by the revocable transfer on death deed."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5664, California Probate Code, deed void if held in joint tenancy or community property with right of survivorship (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5664.)
  "(a) Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 applies to a revocable transfer on death deed of community property. (b) For the purpose of application of Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 to a revocable transfer on death deed of community property, written consent to the deed, revocation of written consent to the deed, or modification of the deed, is ineffective unless recorded within the time required by that chapter for execution or service of the written consent, revocation, or modification."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5666, California Probate Code, community property consent and timing requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5666.)
  Known gap: This is California's specific statutory treatment; it was verified directly from the statute's text rather than assumed. The deed is void under this rule only if the survivorship co-ownership is still in place at the owner's death — for example, if the owner is the first joint tenant or spouse to die. Other states with a TOD/beneficiary deed statute may treat co-owned property differently, and this is not a claim about which state's rule applies to a given property.

CREDITOR CLAIMS AND MEDI-CAL RECOVERY EXPOSURE
Passing outside probate does not shield the property from claims against Pat Morgan's estate. For purposes of Medi-Cal eligibility, executing and recording this deed is not treated as a lifetime transfer of the property, and the property remains subject to claims by the California Department of Health Care Services to the extent otherwise authorized by law. More generally, Jordan Morgan may be personally liable — capped at the fair market value of the property received, minus any liens and encumbrances on it — for Pat Morgan's unsecured debts, and a creditor holding a lien on the property recorded at Pat Morgan's death has priority over that property superior to any of Jordan Morgan's own creditors.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) For the purpose of determination of eligibility for health care under Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 14000) or Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 14200) of Part 3 of Division 9 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, execution and recordation of a revocable transfer on death deed is not a lifetime transfer of the property. (b) Property transferred by a revocable transfer on death deed is subject to claims of the State Department of Health Care Services to the extent authorized by law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5654, California Probate Code, Medi-Cal eligibility and Department of Health Care Services claims (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5654.)
  "Notwithstanding any other statute governing priorities among creditors, a creditor of the transferor whose right is evidenced at the time of the transferor’s death by an encumbrance or lien of record on property transferred by a revocable transfer on death deed has priority against the property over a creditor of the beneficiary, regardless of whether the beneficiary’s obligation was created before or after the transferor’s death and regardless of whether the obligation is secured or unsecured, voluntary or involuntary, recorded or unrecorded."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5670, California Probate Code, lien-holder priority over property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5670.)
  "Each beneficiary is personally liable to the extent provided in Section 5674 for the unsecured debts of the transferor. Any such debt may be enforced against the beneficiary in the same manner as it could have been enforced against the transferor if the transferor had not died."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5672, California Probate Code, beneficiary personal liability for transferor's unsecured debts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5672.)
  "(b) The personal liability of a beneficiary under Section 5672 shall not exceed the fair market value at the time of the transferor’s death of the property received by the beneficiary pursuant to the revocable transfer on death deed, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the property at that time."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5674(b), California Probate Code, cap on beneficiary's liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5674.)
  Known gap: The Medi-Cal-specific provision confirms that recording this deed does not remove the property from Department of Health Care Services claims, but it does so by cross-reference ("to the extent authorized by law") rather than by spelling out the mechanics of Medi-Cal estate recovery itself — those mechanics live in the Welfare and Institutions Code, outside this Probate Code part, and were not independently traced in this research; that narrower point is disclosed honestly rather than guessed at. The general creditor-liability provisions (personal liability capped at property value received, and lien-holder priority) are separately and directly codified. This is California's statutory scheme specifically; whether transferred property remains reachable by creditors or a state Medicaid-recovery program after a similar deed varies by state and is not assumed to be uniform.

SIGNATURE, WITNESSES, AND NOTARIAL ACKNOWLEDGMENT
SIGNATURE AND DATE: Pat Morgan signs and dates this deed below; the name should exactly match the name shown on the property's title documents.

Signature of Pat Morgan: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

WITNESSES: This deed is signed by two witnesses, present together at the same time, who witness Pat Morgan's signing of this deed or Pat Morgan's acknowledgment that it is Pat Morgan's deed. Witness signatures do not need to be notarized.

Witness #1 — Print and sign name: _________________________ Date: _______________

Witness #2 — Print and sign name: _________________________ Date: _______________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF NOTARY: A notary public or other officer completing this certificate verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document to which this certificate is attached, and not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

State of California ) County of _________________________ )

On _________________________ before me, _________________________ (here insert name and title of the officer), personally appeared _________________________, who proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the person(s) whose name(s) is/are subscribed to the within instrument and acknowledged to me that they executed the same in their authorized capacity(ies), and that by their signature(s) on the instrument the person(s), or the entity upon behalf of which the person(s) acted, executed the instrument. I certify under PENALTY OF PERJURY under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing paragraph is true and correct.

WITNESS my hand and official seal.

Signature: _________________________ (Seal)

IMPORTANT NOTICE: This deed must be recorded in the county where the property is located on or before 60 days after the date it is notarized, or it will not be effective.

The "if every beneficiary fails to survive, the deed has no effect" consequence is drawn from the statute's own mandated explanatory form text rather than from the numbered operative subsections alone. This is California's rule; other states' TOD-deed statutes are not assumed to handle predeceased beneficiaries the same way.

expectedJSON.body: If this deed and another instrument (such as a will) both purport to dispose of the same property, and the other instrument makes a revocable disposition of it, whichever of the two was executed later controls. If the other instrument instead makes an irrevocable disposition of the property, that instrument controls regardless of which was executed later. California's statutory TOD deed form itself states that a TOD deed cannot be revoked by a will.

citations.quote: (a) If a revocable transfer on death deed recorded on or before 60 days after the date it was acknowledged before a notary public and another instrument both purport to dispose of the same property: (1) If the other instrument makes a revocable disposition of the property, the later executed of the revocable transfer on death deed or the other instrument is the operative instrument. (2) If the other instrument makes an irrevocable disposition of the property, the other instrument and not the revocable transfer on death deed is the operative instrument.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, statutory form — TOD deed not revocable by will
citations.quote: A TOD deed cannot be revoked by will, or by purporting to leave the subject property to anyone via will.

expectedJSON.gap: California's operative priority rule (Probate Code § 5660) refers generically to "another instrument" that makes a "revocable" or "irrevocable" disposition — it does not use the word "will" in its own text. A will is generally a revocable disposition under California law, which is why the general later-executed-controls rule is described here as applying to wills, but that characterization is an inference from the general nature of wills, not a direct quotation of § 5660 itself. Separately, the statute's own mandated form language does state directly, in its own words, that a TOD deed cannot be revoked by a will. This is California's rule; other states' TOD/beneficiary-deed statutes may resolve a deed-versus-will conflict differently, or may not address it at all.

expectedJSON.body: If, at Pat Morgan's death, title to the property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 is held in joint tenancy or as community property with right of survivorship, this deed is void, and the property instead passes according to the right of survivorship. If Pat Morgan holds the property as community property with a spouse, additional statutory requirements governing spousal consent, revocation of consent, or modification of a community-property TOD deed also apply, and are ineffective unless recorded within the time otherwise required for that consent, revocation, or modification.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, deed void if held in joint tenancy or community property with right of survivorship
citations.quote: If, at the time of the transferor’s death, title to the property described in the revocable transfer on death deed is held in joint tenancy or as community property with right of survivorship, the revocable transfer on death deed is void. The transferor’s interest in the property is governed by the right of survivorship and not by the revocable transfer on death deed.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, community property consent and timing requirements
citations.quote: (a) Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 applies to a revocable transfer on death deed of community property. (b) For the purpose of application of Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 to a revocable transfer on death deed of community property, written consent to the deed, revocation of written consent to the deed, or modification of the deed, is ineffective unless recorded within the time required by that chapter for execution or service of the written consent, revocation, or modification.

expectedJSON.gap: This is California's specific statutory treatment; it was verified directly from the statute's text rather than assumed. The deed is void under this rule only if the survivorship co-ownership is still in place at the owner's death — for example, if the owner is the first joint tenant or spouse to die. Other states with a TOD/beneficiary deed statute may treat co-owned property differently, and this is not a claim about which state's rule applies to a given property.

expectedJSON.body: Passing outside probate does not shield the property from claims against Pat Morgan's estate. For purposes of Medi-Cal eligibility, executing and recording this deed is not treated as a lifetime transfer of the property, and the property remains subject to claims by the California Department of Health Care Services to the extent otherwise authorized by law. More generally, Jordan Morgan may be personally liable — capped at the fair market value of the property received, minus any liens and encumbrances on it — for Pat Morgan's unsecured debts, and a creditor holding a lien on the property recorded at Pat Morgan's death has priority over that property superior to any of Jordan Morgan's own creditors.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, Medi-Cal eligibility and Department of Health Care Services claims
citations.quote: (a) For the purpose of determination of eligibility for health care under Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 14000) or Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 14200) of Part 3 of Division 9 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, execution and recordation of a revocable transfer on death deed is not a lifetime transfer of the property. (b) Property transferred by a revocable transfer on death deed is subject to claims of the State Department of Health Care Services to the extent authorized by law.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, lien-holder priority over property
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other statute governing priorities among creditors, a creditor of the transferor whose right is evidenced at the time of the transferor’s death by an encumbrance or lien of record on property transferred by a revocable transfer on death deed has priority against the property over a creditor of the beneficiary, regardless of whether the beneficiary’s obligation was created before or after the transferor’s death and regardless of whether the obligation is secured or unsecured, voluntary or involuntary, recorded or unrecorded.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, beneficiary personal liability for transferor's unsecured debts
citations.quote: Each beneficiary is personally liable to the extent provided in Section 5674 for the unsecured debts of the transferor. Any such debt may be enforced against the beneficiary in the same manner as it could have been enforced against the transferor if the transferor had not died.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, cap on beneficiary's liability
citations.quote: (b) The personal liability of a beneficiary under Section 5672 shall not exceed the fair market value at the time of the transferor’s death of the property received by the beneficiary pursuant to the revocable transfer on death deed, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the property at that time.

expectedJSON.gap: The Medi-Cal-specific provision confirms that recording this deed does not remove the property from Department of Health Care Services claims, but it does so by cross-reference ("to the extent authorized by law") rather than by spelling out the mechanics of Medi-Cal estate recovery itself — those mechanics live in the Welfare and Institutions Code, outside this Probate Code part, and were not independently traced in this research; that narrower point is disclosed honestly rather than guessed at. The general creditor-liability provisions (personal liability capped at property value received, and lien-holder priority) are separately and directly codified. This is California's statutory scheme specifically; whether transferred property remains reachable by creditors or a state Medicaid-recovery program after a similar deed varies by state and is not assumed to be uniform.
